questions.explanation: Antonio Toledo was the premier Neoclassical/Beaux-Arts architect among the pensionado generation. His Manila City Hall is the Philippine government's most iconic Neoclassical building — featuring symmetrical facades, classical columns, pediments, and a monumental central tower. This reflects the American colonial preference for Neoclassicism as the appropriate architectural language for democratic government institutions. Toledo's other major works include: National Museum (Leyte Capitol), Cebu Provincial Capitol, Bureau of Customs, and Department of Tourism Building.

questions.explanation: Carlos Barretto (Drexel University, graduated 1908) is historically significant as the FIRST pensionado architect to complete an American architecture degree. This predates Tomas Mapua (Cornell, 1911), Juan Arellano (Penn Academy/Drexel, 1911), and Antonio Toledo (Ohio State, 1911). Barretto's career: (1) Second registered architect in the Philippines (after Mapua); (2) Pioneered the Division of Architecture at the Bureau of Public Works; (3) Organized the Philippine Institute of Architects after WWII; (4) Designed Art Deco Carnival infrastructures for the 1935 Philippine Carnival.

questions.explanation: The American colonial period (1898–1946) introduced fundamentally new building technologies: (1) REINFORCED CONCRETE (terroconcrete) — concrete with embedded steel reinforcement; (2) STEEL-FRAMED SKELETON CONSTRUCTION — steel columns and beams form a structural frame; (3) KAHN TRUSS SYSTEM — trussed bars within concrete molds for floor slabs and beams; (4) CONCRETE HOLLOW BLOCKS (CHB) — standardized modular concrete blocks that became the standard wall material.

questions.explanation: The 1901 McMillan Plan (authored by Burnham, Daniel Chester French, and the McMillan Commission) reorganized Washington D.C.'s National Mall — removing Victorian-era structures, restoring the L'Enfant plan, and creating the iconic view from the Capitol Building to the Washington Monument. Burnham applied the same conceptual logic to Manila: (1) Create a grand civic axis from the Rizal Monument (south) to the planned Philippine Capitol Building (north); (2) Connect the civic center to the waterfront (Manila Bay); (3) Establish a park system and radial boulevards. The key formal analogy: Washington Monument (column/obelisk) axis → Rizal Monument (column/obelisk) axis; U.S. Capitol (government building) → planned Philippine Capitol (government building).

questions.explanation: Burnham's 1905 Manila plan envisioned a grand civic axis: the Rizal Monument at the south end, the Philippine Capitol Building at the north end, connected by a grand boulevard. However, the Capitol Building was never constructed due to: (1) Funding constraints — the U.S. colonial government prioritized other infrastructure; (2) Policy changes toward Commonwealth status. What WAS built: Roxas Boulevard (bayshore drive), radial avenues from Luneta, the park system, waterfront promenades. The unbuilt Capitol remains the most significant unrealized element of Burnham's vision.

questions.explanation: Pablo Antonio's FEU (Far Eastern University) Campus is his masterwork and the largest surviving ensemble of Art Deco architecture in Manila. Built between 1938 and 1950, the campus features Antonio's signature 'clean lines, plain surfaces, and bold rectangular masses' — a radical departure from Neoclassicism. The FEU Campus received a UNESCO Asia-Pacific Heritage Awards Honorable Mention in 2005. Antonio also designed multiple Manila theaters — Ideal Theater, Life Theater (1941), Scala Theater, Lyric Theater, and Forum Theater.
